title: Optimal Line-Ups Near Weight $n/2$ Outperform Maximum-Weight Matchings by a Constant Gap, Refuting Theorem 4(2) of arXiv:2605.21234
abstract: In the Team Order problem of arXiv:2605.21234, Theorem 4(2) asserted that whenever a maximum-weight matching $M^*$ has weight near $n/2$, any optimal line-up exceeds $M^*$ in winning probability by at most $\frac{4 + o(1)}{n+1} \sum_{e \in M^*} (p_e - 1/2)^2$. We show that this claim is false for every choice of the $o(1)$ term. On a $(2m+3)$-player instance, the identity matching has all edge probabilities equal to $1/2$, making it a maximum-weight matching of weight $n/2$ with winning probability $1/2$ and zero claimed error, while a cyclic rotation line-up wins with probability $9/16$. Furthermore, in a strengthened $(2m+3)$-player instance, the all-$1/2$ identity matching is the unique maximum-weight matching, yet the rotation line-up wins with probability at least $1/2 + 1/40$, refuting even the existential formulation of the theorem. All of these results, culminating in `team_thm4_part2_false` and `team_thm4_part2_exists_false`, are verified in Lean.
introduction:
In the Team Order problem introduced in arXiv:2605.21234, two teams compete across $n$ positions. A line-up of team 1 against a fixed line-up of team 2 corresponds to a perfect matching, formalised as a permutation $\pi$ of the $n$ positions, where player $i$ of team 1 faces player $\pi(i)$ of team 2 (`team_weight`). Each individual match is resolved independently, with team 1 winning against player $\pi(i)$ with probability $p(i, \pi(i))$. The weight of a line-up $\pi$ is its expected number of wins, $w(\pi) = \sum_{i} p(i, \pi(i))$ (`team_weight`). Team 1 wins the team contest if it wins at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ of the $n$ matches (`team_winProb`). A line-up is optimal if it maximizes this overall winning probability (`team_isOptimal`).

In Section 6 of arXiv:2605.21234, Theorem 4(2) addressed the relationship between a maximum-weight matching and an optimal line-up when the expected score is close to balanced. Specifically, the theorem claimed that for every maximum-weight matching $M^*$ whose weight satisfies $w(M^*) \in [n/2 - \sqrt{n}\log n, n/2 + \sqrt{n}\log n]$, every optimal line-up $O$ satisfies
$$ \Pr[O \text{ wins}] \le \Pr[M^* \text{ wins}] + \frac{4 + o(1)}{n+1} \sum_{e \in M^*} \left(p_e - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2. $$
When formalized as `team_thm4_part2`, this assertion states that for any sequence $\varepsilon : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ representing the $o(1)$ term and any threshold $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the bound holds for all instances with $n \ge N$.

This post presents the formal refutation of this theorem in `team_thm4_part2_false`. We exhibit an explicit $(2m+3)$-player instance where the identity matching is a maximum-weight matching with all edge probabilities equal to $1/2$, so the claimed error term vanishes entirely and the identity line-up wins with probability $1/2$. An alternative rotation line-up wins with probability $9/16$, revealing a persistent gap of $1/16$. In addition, we present a strengthened instance where the all-$1/2$ line-up is the unique maximum-weight matching and the rotation line-up wins with probability at least $1/2 + 1/40$, refuting even the existential interpretation of the claim in `team_thm4_part2_exists_false`.
result:
The main theorem, `team_thm4_part2_false`, refutes Theorem 4(2) of arXiv:2605.21234. For any function $\varepsilon : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ representing the $o(1)$ term and any cutoff $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the property `team_thm4_part2` fails: there exists an instance with $n \ge N$ players, a maximum-weight matching $M^*$ with weight $w(M^*) \in [n/2 - \sqrt{n}\log n, n/2 + \sqrt{n}\log n]$, and an optimal line-up $O$ such that
$$ \Pr[O \text{ wins}] > \Pr[M^* \text{ wins}] + \frac{4 + \varepsilon(n)}{n+1} \sum_{e \in M^*} \left(p_e - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2. $$
On the $(2m+3)$-player instance, the identity matching $M^*$ has all edge probabilities equal to $1/2$, so $w(M^*) = n/2$ and $\sum_{e \in M^*} (p_e - 1/2)^2 = 0$. While $M^*$ wins with probability $1/2$, the optimal line-up wins with probability at least $9/16$.

In Lean, the theorem `team_thm4_part2_false` quantifies universally over the candidate error function $\varepsilon : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and cutoff $N : \mathbb{N}$, asserting the negation of `team_thm4_part2` $\varepsilon$ $N$ without restricting the instances beyond $n \ge N$.

The further theorem, `team_thm4_part2_exists_false`, strengthens this refutation to the existential reading of the claim. In `team_thm4_part2`, the bound is stated for every maximum-weight matching $M^*$. One might ask whether the claim could hold if weakened to assert that there exists some maximum-weight matching satisfying the bound. Theorem `team_thm4_part2_exists_false` shows that even this existential version fails for every $\varepsilon : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every cutoff $N \in \mathbb{N}$: on a strengthened $(2m+3)$-player instance, the all-$1/2$ identity matching is the unique maximum-weight matching, so the quadratic error term is $0$, yet the optimal line-up wins with probability at least $1/2 + 1/40$.
proof:
The refutation proceeds by constructing explicit instances of the Team Order problem of size $n = 2m + 3$, chosen large enough so that $n \ge N$.

To prove `team_thm4_part2_false`, we define the instance `team_P` on $n$ players. The probability matrix assigns $p(i, i) = 1/2$ along the diagonal, $p(i, (i+1) \bmod n) = \text{team\_w}(i)$ on the cyclic superdiagonal, and $0$ on all other entries. Lemma `team_P_bounds` verifies that all entries of `team_P` lie in the interval $[0, 1]$.

We analyze two line-ups in `team_P`. Under the identity line-up $\pi(i) = i$, each player meets the corresponding opponent with probability $1/2$. Lemma `team_weight_id` computes its weight as $w(\pi) = n/2$, which satisfies the condition $w(\pi) \in [n/2 - \sqrt{n}\log n, n/2 + \sqrt{n}\log n]$. Lemma `team_id_maxWeight` establishes that the identity line-up is a maximum-weight matching in `team_P`. Lemma `team_id_winProb` shows that this line-up wins the team contest with probability exactly $1/2$. Because each edge $e$ in the identity matching has $p_e = 1/2$, the sum $\sum_{e \in M^*} (p_e - 1/2)^2$ is identically $0$. Hence, the upper bound asserted by `team_thm4_part2` reduces to $1/2$.

Next, we consider the rotation line-up $\pi(i) = (i+1) \bmod n$. Lemma `team_rot_winProb` evaluates the distribution of individual match outcomes under this permutation and proves that it wins the team contest with probability $9/16$. Because an optimal line-up (`team_isOptimal`) achieves at least the winning probability of any specific line-up, its winning probability is at least $9/16$. Since $9/16 > 1/2$, the claimed upper bound fails by at least $1/16$, completing the proof of `team_thm4_part2_false`.

To prove `team_thm4_part2_exists_false`, we eliminate the possibility that another maximum-weight matching could satisfy the bound. We construct the strengthened instance `team_P2` on $n = 2m + 3$ players, defined by $p(i, i) = 1/2$, $p(i, (i+1) \bmod n) = 1/2 - v'_i + v'_{i+1} - \tau$, and $0$ elsewhere. Lemma `team_P2_bounds` confirms that all entries are valid probabilities in $[0, 1]$.

In `team_P2`, lemma `team_weight2_id` verifies that the identity line-up has weight $n/2$. Lemma `team2_unique_maxWeight` proves that the identity line-up is the unique maximum-weight matching of the strengthened instance. Lemma `team_id_winProb2` confirms that this line-up wins with probability exactly $1/2$. Since it is the unique maximum-weight matching and all its edge probabilities are $1/2$, the quadratic penalty term must vanish for any candidate maximum-weight matching. Finally, lemma `team_rot_winProb2` proves that the rotation line-up achieves a winning probability of at least $1/2 + 1/40$. The optimal line-up therefore beats the unique maximum-weight matching by at least $1/40$, establishing `team_thm4_part2_exists_false`.
discussion:
The results provide explicit counterexamples refuting Theorem 4(2) of arXiv:2605.21234. In relation to the claim as originally posed, the counterexamples demonstrate that the upper bound cannot hold for any sequence $\varepsilon(n)$ playing the role of $o(1)$, nor for any threshold $N$.

The counterexamples operate in the regime where the maximum-weight matching has weight exactly $n/2$. In this setting, when all edge probabilities in $M^*$ equal $1/2$, the quadratic penalty $\sum_{e \in M^*} (p_e - 1/2)^2$ vanishes, forcing the upper bound in Theorem 4(2) to equal $\Pr[M^* \text{ wins}] = 1/2$. However, alternative line-ups achieve strictly larger winning probabilities: $9/16$ in `team_P`, and at least $1/2 + 1/40$ in `team_P2`.

The counterexample in `team_thm4_part2_false` disproves the universal formulation of the bound across all maximum-weight matchings, while `team_thm4_part2_exists_false` shows that weakening the claim to an existential statement—asserting the existence of at least one maximum-weight matching satisfying the bound—also fails, since the identity matching is the unique maximum-weight matching in `team_P2`. Both families of instances are constructed for odd dimensions $n = 2m + 3$. The material does not address other assertions of Theorem 4 or conditions under which an amended bound could be established.
